props.title: Jennifer's Body
props.initialSlug: Demonic cheerleader devours high school boys

sections.content: Jennifer's Body (2009) brilliantly subverts horror tropes by weaponizing the female monster against toxic masculinity. Diablo Cody's razor-sharp script pairs perfectly with Karyn Kusama's direction, creating a feminist horror-comedy that was wildly ahead of its time. Like Ginger Snaps (2000) before it, the film uses supernatural transformation as a metaphor for female sexuality and rage. The marketing tragically mishandled it as mere Megan Fox eye candy, when it's actually a savage critique of how society treats young women.

sections.content: The film sits at a crucial intersection between teen horror and feminist revenge narratives that would later flourish in films like Raw (2016) and Fresh (2022). Its influence can be seen in recent horror hits that center female rage, like Promising Young Woman (2020) and Ready or Not (2019). The dynamic between Jennifer and Needy also paved the way for more complex female friendships in horror, exploring how patriarchal systems often pit women against each other.

The film's commentary on sacrifice and the music industry feels especially prescient today. The demonic band Low Shoulder's exploitation of Jennifer mirrors real-world cases of powerful men preying on young women in entertainment. This theme would later be explored in films like A Star Is Born (2018) and Her Smell (2018), though Jennifer's Body adds a supernatural vengeance element that's uniquely satisfying. sections.content: The film's reputation has undergone a massive transformation since its release. Initially dismissed as a failed teen horror flick, it's now celebrated as a queer cult classic and feminist touchstone. Its exploration of female friendship, sexuality, and rage resonates strongly with modern audiences, particularly in the post-#MeToo era. The film shares DNA with Heathers (1988) and Tragedy Girls (2017) in its dark approach to teen dynamics and female violence.
